paragraphs.source_en: Why would the hunter-gatherers depict domesticated animals? One hypothesis is that they depicted cattle belonging to the herders occupying the same region. However, it cannot be excluded that the hunters represented their own domesticated animals which started to enter into their economy. The long coexistence with the pastoralists must have had an impact on the hunters who had the choice and ability to adopt domesticated animals as well. This hypothesis may be confirmed by another outstanding painting from the same site, namely a painting of large, circa 1 m tall, isolated cattle horns in the shape of a lyre typical for domesticated animals, and in a pure Round Head style (Fig 4-8). The animal's body is completely missing and it is probable that originally only the horns were actually painted because they are well preserved whereas there is no trace of the rest of the animal.

paragraphs.source_en: The dominant position of the horns in the central part of the wall indicates their importance. They are located near paintings of mouflon (Fig. 4-9), therefore suggesting their significance in the ideology. Could the paintings at Uan Mata indicate the increasing importance of animals other than wild ones and could they confirm a gradual transition from hunting-gathering to an economy based on domestic cattle? And if so, why are there not more examples of domesticated animals in the Round Head style?

paragraphs.source_en: The interaction of hunters with herders is known from the ethnographic record. The spread of farming and herding over vast areas of eastern and southern Africa once occupied exclusively by hunters and gatherers encompassed a number of different culture-contact situations, with varying outcomes for the hunters (Brooks et al. 1984). Some groups were totally assimilated into the societies of the expanding farmers or herders, leaving no living traces of their existence other than in the gene pools or languages of the assimilators. However, in areas less desirable for farming and herding, a small minority of hunting populations preserved a distinct identity through many years of contact, often relating to farmers or herders as a distinct caste of traders, hunters, or smiths or as a lower class of servants (Brooks et al. 1984).
